deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the surrounding pages): alpha(x,y,z) is a stationary temperature with gradient (p,q,r) = grad alpha. It satisfies curl-freeness (q_z = r_y, r_x = p_z, p_y = q_x) and Laplace's equation p_x + q_y + r_z = 0. The standing hypothesis is that the isothermal surfaces alpha = const coincide with the surfaces m = p^2+q^2+r^2 = const, i.e. |grad alpha|^2 is a function of alpha. Riemann sorts the cases by the functional rank of (p,q,r):
- Case 1 (rank 3, previous page): concentric spheres.
- Case 2 (rank 2, this page): leads to coaxial circular cylinders, finished on the next page.
- Case 3 (rank 1): impossible.
- Case 4 (rank 0): parallel planes.

Case 2. There is one relation r = r(p,q); write a = r_p, b = r_q, so a_q = b_p.

(i) Derivation of the first-order PDE [filled in by me]. From dr = a dp + b dq we get r_x = a p_x + b q_x. Curl-freeness gives r_x = p_z and q_x = p_y, hence p_z = a p_x + b p_y. Likewise q_z = r_y = a p_y + b q_y = a q_x + b q_y. Finally r_z = a p_z + b q_z = a r_x + b r_y. So every function F of (p,q) satisfies F_z = a F_x + b F_y.

(ii) Suppose m is not constant (8). Then alpha, being a function of m, depends only on (p,q). The rule F_z = a F_x + b F_y applied to alpha gives r = a p + b q, so r is homogeneous of degree 1 in (p,q). Differentiating r = ap + bq:
- with respect to p: p a_p + q b_p = 0;
- with respect to q: p a_q + q b_q = 0.
Since (p,q) is not zero, the determinant vanishes: a_p b_q - a_q b_p = 0 (9). This is the vanishing Hessian of r(p,q): the surface r = r(p,q) in (p,q,r)-space is a cone, hence developable.

(iii) Legendre-type transform, valid also when (8) holds. Set s = alpha - xp - yq - zr. Then ds = -x dp - y dq - z dr = -(x+az) dp - (y+bz) dq. So s = s(p,q), with s_p = -(x+az) and s_q = -(y+bz) (10).

(iv) Change of independent variables to (p,q,z), so that x = x(p,q,z) and y = y(p,q,z).
- Inverting the Jacobian at fixed z, with D = x_p y_q - x_q y_p: p_x = y_q/D, q_y = x_p/D.
- From 0 = x_p p_z + x_q q_z + x_z and the analogous y-equation: p_z = -(y_q x_z - x_q y_z)/D and q_z = -(x_p y_z - y_p x_z)/D.
- Using r_z = a p_z + b q_z and multiplying by D, Laplace's equation becomes x_p + y_q - a(y_q x_z - x_q y_z) - b(x_p y_z - y_p x_z) = 0.

Now insert x = -s_p - a z and y = -s_q - b z, so x_z = -a and y_z = -b. The equation becomes (1+b^2) x_p + (1+a^2) y_q - ab(x_q + y_p) = 0, that is:
z[(1+b^2) a_p - ab(a_q + b_p) + (1+a^2) b_q] + (1+b^2) s_pp - 2ab s_pq + (1+a^2) s_qq = 0.

(v) Since a, b, s do not depend on z, the bracket and the remainder vanish separately:
- (11): (1+b^2) s_pp - 2ab s_pq + (1+a^2) s_qq = 0.
- (12): (1+b^2) a_p - ab(a_q+b_p) + (1+a^2) b_q = 0. Since a = r_p, b = r_q, this is (1+r_q^2) r_pp - 2 r_p r_q r_pq + (1+r_p^2) r_qq = 0, the minimal surface equation for r = r(p,q).

(vi) Viewing (p,q,r) as Cartesian coordinates, the image surface is minimal. By (8) it would also be a sphere, which is impossible since a sphere is not minimal. By (9) it is developable (K = 0), and K = H = 0 forces a plane. So a and b are constants; the plane passes through the origin because r = ap + bq. Rotating the axes gives a = b = 0, i.e. r = 0, and (11) becomes s_pp + s_qq = 0 (13).

(vii) As in case 1, the requirement that alpha = s - p s_p - q s_q be a function of m = p^2+q^2 gives s = psi(m) + p chi(q/p) [justification mine]:
- psi(m) contributes psi - 2m psi', a function of m;
- p chi(q/p) is homogeneous of degree 1 and drops out.
With beta = q/p:
- -x = s_p = 2p psi'(m) + chi(beta) - beta chi'(beta);
- -y = s_q = 2q psi'(m) + chi'(beta).

The next page substitutes this into (13), obtaining sqrt(m)(4psi' + 4m psi'') + (1+beta^2)^(3/2) chi'' = 0. Separating variables yields chi = k sqrt(1+beta^2) + a + b beta, so the isotherms are circular cylinders with a common axis. Overall the page belongs to the classification of harmonic functions whose level surfaces have constant |grad| (isoparametric families in R^3): planes, concentric spheres, coaxial cylinders.
errors: The text says the step to the z-separated equation is made 'mit Hülfe von (9.)', but (9) is not needed. After multiplying through by the Jacobian D, the computation is purely algebraic and produces no z^2 terms. The reference is harmless but superfluous.
The bracket in the displayed z{...] equation is mismatched: it opens with a brace and closes with a square bracket. This is a notational slip only.
Implicit step: concluding from ds = -(x+az)dp - (y+bz)dq that s depends only on (p,q) uses the rank-2 hypothesis. This is correct but unstated.

Implicit step: the ansatz s = psi(m) + p chi(q/p) is justified only by 'wie im ersten Fall'. It follows from requiring that alpha = s - p s_p - q s_q be a function of m, which is correct (general solution = particular solution + homogeneous degree-1 function).

Excluding the sphere case (8) relies on the fact that a sphere is not a minimal surface. This is correct but not stated explicitly. The (8) case is handled correctly because (10)-(12) were derived without assuming alpha = alpha(p,q).

results.what: For a harmonic function alpha whose gradient components satisfy one functional relation r = r(p,q), the relation surface in gradient space satisfies the minimal surface equation (via the Legendre-type transform s = alpha - x.grad alpha).
results.modern_name: Hodograph/Legendre transform of the Laplace equation; gradient image of harmonic functions of rank 2 is a minimal surface
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre-transform technique: Legendre/Ampère; hodograph methods for potential flows: Molenbroek, Chaplygin (1890s)

results.what: A surface that is both minimal and developable (or both minimal and spherical) is a plane.
results.modern_name: K = 0 and H = 0 imply a plane

results.what: Homogeneity r = ap + bq implies vanishing Hessian, so r(p,q) defines a cone (developable surface).
results.modern_name: Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions; developable surfaces have zero Hessian

results.what: Part of the classification: harmonic alpha with |grad alpha| constant on level sets has level sets that are parallel planes, concentric spheres or coaxial circular cylinders (case 2 here yields cylinders).
results.modern_name: Classification of isoparametric surfaces / isoparametric families in R^3
results.usually_credited_to: Somigliana (1919), Levi-Civita (1937), B. Segre (1938); related isothermal-surface work of Lamé

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out, by an elegant Legendre transform plus a minimal-surface argument, part of the classification of harmonic functions whose isotherms have constant gradient magnitude, i.e. isoparametric families in R^3. That theorem is usually attributed to Somigliana (1919) and Levi-Civita/Segre (1937-38). The heat-conduction setting (isotherms invariant in time) was a classical 19th-century topic, though, and the Riemann Nachlass on heat conduction is partly known through Weber's editorial work. The handwriting may also be a copy by another hand, so authorship and novelty are uncertain. The result is notable but not certainly unknown.

transcription_corrections: 'so werden a von denselben beiden Variablen abhängen' should read 'so wird α von denselben beiden Variablen abhängen'. It is the temperature alpha, a function of m, that depends on (p,q); this is what gives r = ap + bq.
In (9) the manuscript shows a struck-out symbol after ∂b/∂q (a cancelled ∂); the intended formula is a_p b_q - a_q b_p = 0.
'zugleich einen Kugel' should be 'zugleich eine Kugel'.
'Dies kann nur erweislich sein' is an uncertain reading. The sense is 'Dies kann nur [dann der Fall] sein, wenn die Fläche eine Ebene ist'.
Top-left folio marks read '27 30', i.e. an old number 27 replaced by 30, not just '30'.
The expression with a struck '∂z/∂z' in the first term of the a(...) bracket corresponds to ∂x/∂z; the corrected reading in the transcription is right.
